questions.q: What does SET STATISTICS TIME print?
options: CPU time and elapsed time for parsing and execution
The number of rows returned
The execution plan as XML
The names of every index used
questions.explain: It prints two timing breakdowns — one for parsing the query, one for actually running it.

questions.q: If elapsed time is much higher than CPU time, what does that suggest?
options: The query is spending most of its time waiting — on disk I/O, locks, or other contention — not on raw computation
The query returned incorrect results
SQL Server needs to be restarted
The index is corrupted
questions.explain: A large gap between CPU time and elapsed time points to waiting, not CPU work, as the real bottleneck.

questions.q: Why is logical reads usually the preferred metric for proving a tuning change worked?
options: It's stable across runs and directly measures how much work the storage engine did, unlike timing which can jitter with server load
It's the only number SQL Server can report
It measures network latency to the client
It's always exactly equal to physical reads
questions.explain: Timing can vary run to run depending on what else is happening on the server; logical reads is a consistent measure of actual work.

options: Pages that had to be read from disk because they weren't already in the buffer cache
Pages read from memory only
The total number of rows scanned
The number of indexes on a table
questions.explain: Physical reads happen when a needed page isn't cached and SQL Server must fetch it from disk.

questions.q: In the lesson's before/after demo, what proved the covering index actually helped?
options: Logical reads dropped sharply for the same query after adding the index
The query returned more rows
The CPU time became exactly zero
The table was rebuilt
questions.explain: A sharp drop in logical reads for the identical query, before vs. after the index, is direct evidence the change reduced real work.
